claim: A p53 biosensor was constructed using a 150-bp fragment containing a p53 enhancer with a conserved p53 consensus binding site upstream of GFP.
source: A well-characterized p53 enhancer (black line) that contains a p53 consensus binding site (blue box) conserved from flies to humans resides upstream of the reaper locus (gray box) (Brodsky et al., 2000). A 150-bp fragment containing this enhancer was placed upstream of GFP (p53R-GFP).
evidence: The construction is described in the text with reference to prior work (Brodsky et al., 2000) establishing the enhancer's characterization.

claim: Two p53 biosensor transgenic fly strains were created, one with nuclear localization signal (p53R-GFPnls) and one without (p53R-GFPcyt).
source: Transgenic fly strains are made with two reporter constructs, one contains a nuclear localization signal for GFP (p53R-GFPnls) and the other one does not (p53R-GFPcyt).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the creation of two distinct reporter constructs.

claim: The p53 biosensors require wild-type p53 and are effective readouts for p53 function.
source: These biosensors require wild-type p53 and are effective readouts for p53 function.
evidence: The text states this as a property of the biosensors, supported by experimental validation shown in figures.

claim: Germline stem cells (GSCs) undergo self-renewing divisions that produce a GSC and a cystoblast (CB).
source: In the ovary, germline stem cells (GSCs) undergo self-renewing divisions that typically produce a GSC and a cystoblast (CB).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila GSC biology.

claim: GSCs support egg production throughout the lifespan of female adults.
source: These GSCs support egg production throughout the lifespan of female adults (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with reference to a figure.

claim: Programmed p53 activity triggered by meiosis was observed in region 2 of the germarium.
source: As previously described (Lu et al., 2010), programed p53 activity triggered by meiosis was only observed in region 2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This observation is cited from prior work (Lu et al., 2010) and referenced to a figure.

claim: After exposure to ionizing radiation, p53 activity was induced in virtually all germaria.
source: After exposure to ionizing radiation (IR) stress, p53 activity was induced in virtually all germaria.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Despite widespread damage to the ovary after IR, p53 response was restricted to germline stem cells (GSCs) and their immediate progeny (CBs).
source: However, despite widespread damage to the organ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), this unprogrammed response was remarkably restricted to germline stem cells (GSCs) and their immediate progeny (CBs) (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: The text describes the observation with reference to figures showing widespread damage and restricted response.

claim: The IR-induced p53 response in GSCs/CBs was highly penetrant.
source: Furthermore, as seen in Figure 1—source data 1A, this response was highly penetrant.
evidence: The text refers to source data showing the penetrance of the response.

claim: The GFP signal seen in CBs likely reflects perduring GFP from the parental stem cells.
source: Since we rarely observe reporter activation only in CBs, the signal seen in CBs probably reflects GFP perduring from the parental stem cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation pattern.

claim: Post-irradiation levels of GFP were more robust than the programmed activity during meiosis.
source: Furthermore, post-irradiation levels of GFP were noticeably more robust than the programed activity during meiosis (compare solid arrows to open arrows in Figure 1C,D) (Lu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the data with reference to figures.

claim: p53 biosensor activity was not observed within the ovary of p53−/− animals.
source: As expected, p53 biosensor activity was not observed within the ovary of p53−/− animals and was also absent from ovaries lacking the upstream Chk2 kinase (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A′,A′′, Figure 1—source data 1A).
evidence: This is experimental validation showing the biosensor requires p53.

claim: p53 biosensor activity was absent from ovaries lacking the upstream Chk2 kinase.
source: As expected, p53 biosensor activity was not observed within the ovary of p53−/− animals and was also absent from ovaries lacking the upstream Chk2 kinase (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A′,A′′, Figure 1—source data 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data showing Chk2 is required for the biosensor response.

claim: DNA double-stranded breaks (DSBs) are responsible for many of the biological effects associated with IR.
source: Double stranded DNA breaks (DSBs) are responsible for many of the biological effects associated with IR (Ward, 1994).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature (Ward, 1994).

claim: A single DSB induced by I-SceI endonuclease was sufficient to provoke robust p53 activity in GSCs/CBs.
source: Furthermore, it is notable that a single DSB was sufficient to provoke robust p53 activity in GSCs/CBs.
evidence: This is an observation from the I-SceI experiment described in the text.

claim: Whether exogenously imposed or intrinsically engineered, DSBs triggered p53 selective activation confined to GSCs and their immediate progeny.
source: Therefore, whether exogenously imposed or intrinsically engineered, DSBs triggered p53 selective activation that was confined to GSCs and their immediate progeny.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the IR and I-SceI experiments.

claim: The stem cell restricted p53 response is under genetic control.
source: Furthermore, this stem cell restricted response is clearly under genetic control.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that certain mutants lose the restricted response.

claim: In certain mutants, p53 exhibits non-selective action throughout the ovary after IR challenge.
source: For example, in directed tests of chosen mutants we identified a class of lesions that exhibit non-selective p53 action throughout the ovary only after IR challenge (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—source data 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data from mutant analysis.

claim: p53 is present and potentially functional in all cells of the ovary but its action is confined to GSCs and their immediate progeny under normal conditions.
source: Therefore, p53 is present and potentially functional in all cells of the ovary but, under normal conditions, its action is somehow confined to GSCs and their immediate progeny.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutants can show non-selective p53 activity, indicating p53 is present throughout but normally restricted.

claim: Selective p53 reporter activation was observed in GSCs and their immediate progeny (gonioblasts) in irradiated testis.
source: As seen in the ovary, we observed selective p53 reporter activation in GSCs and their immediate progeny (gonioblasts) in irradiated testis (Figure 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from male germline analysis.

claim: Stimulus-dependent p53 activity in testis required p53 and was not seen in unchallenged testis.
source: Likewise, stimulus-dependent activity required p53 and was not seen in unchallenged testis (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 1—source data 1A).
evidence: This is experimental validation data.

claim: The p53 biosensor was occasionally present in early spermatogonial cysts, possibly reflecting perduring GFP and/or independent activation associated with dying cells.
source: Occasionally, the biosensor was also present in early spermatogonial cysts, perhaps reflecting perduring GFP and/or independent activation associated with dying cells (Figure 2D–D′′, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E′′).
evidence: This is an observation with speculative interpretation.

claim: Selective p53 activation in the stem cell compartment is a general property of germline tissues exposed to genotoxic stress.
source: Collectively, the observations in Figure 1 and Figure 2 demonstrate that selective p53 activation in the stem cell compartment is a general property of germline tissues exposed to genotoxic stress.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from observations in both ovary and testis.

claim: Perturbation-dependent induction of the p53 biosensor in gonadal stem cells was highly penetrant.
source: We note that perturbation-dependent induction of the p53 biosensor in gonadal stem cells was highly penetrant (Figure 1E, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated based on quantitative data in the figures.

claim: The strength of p53 biosensor signal and the number of responding cells were variable from animal to animal.
source: However, like all stress responses, the strength of signal and the number of responding cells were variable from animal to animal (Figure 1C,D, Figure 2D) perhaps reflecting distinct cell cycle dynamics occurring in GSCs at the time of challenge.
evidence: This is an observation with speculative interpretation about the cause.

claim: In cutoff mutants, induction of p53R-GFP occurs exclusively in GSCs and their progeny at a penetrance comparable to irradiated wild-type animals.
source: Figure 3A shows that in cutoff mutants induction of p53R-GFP occurs exclusively in GSCs and their progeny at a penetrance comparable to irradiated wild-type animals (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from cutoff mutant analysis.

claim: Frequent p53 activation in the germline was observed in the GSCs of aubergine mutants.
source: Frequent p53 activation in the germline was similarly observed in the GSCs of aubergine mutants (Figure 3B) and rad54 mutants defective for DNA repair (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is experimental data from aubergine mutant analysis.

claim: Frequent p53 activation in the germline was observed in the GSCs of rad54 mutants defective for DNA repair.
source: Frequent p53 activation in the germline was similarly observed in the GSCs of aubergine mutants (Figure 3B) and rad54 mutants defective for DNA repair (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is experimental data from rad54 mutant analysis.

claim: In aubergine and rad54 mutants, the p53 biosensor was not entirely restricted to GSCs/CBs.
source: However, in contrast to cutoff mutants, the p53 biosensor was not entirely restricted to GSCs/CBs in these mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C, Figure 3—source data 1) perhaps reflecting differences in the kinetics of repair that may occur in these different backgrounds (Klattenhoff et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an observation with speculative interpretation citing prior work.

claim: Cutoff and aubergine encode essential components of the piwi-associated RNA (piRNA) pathway that silence retrotransposons in the germline.
source: These genes encode essential components of the piwi-associated RNA (piRNA) pathway, acting to silence retrotransposons in the germline (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature (Chen et al., 2007).

claim: Cutoff and aubergine mutants exhibit disregulated retrotransposition, reduced fecundity, and egg shell ventralization.
source: The corresponding mutants exhibit disregulated retrotransposition, reduced fecundity, and egg shell ventralization (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature (Chen et al., 2007).

claim: In somatic cells, Dp53 promotes stress-induced apoptosis.
source: In somatic cells, Dp53 promotes stress-induced apoptosis (Sogame et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature (Sogame et al., 2003).

claim: In the 24-hr period post IR challenge, over 90% of GSCs induce the p53 reporter but the average incidence of apoptosis was less than 4%.
source: In the 24-hr period post challenge, over 90% of GSCs induce the reporter but the average incidence of apoptosis was less than 4% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 1A).
evidence: This is quantitative data from apoptosis analysis.

claim: No obvious role for p53 in regulating stem cell numbers in the Drosophila ovary was observed in the presence or absence of stress.
source: Furthermore, we did not observe an obvious role for p53 in regulating stem cell numbers in the Drosophila ovary in the presence or absence of stress (Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 4—source data 1A).
evidence: This is a negative result from experimental observation.

claim: Resolution of DSBs after IR was unaffected in the germaria of p53 mutants.
source: We also used α-pH2Av immunostaining, the Drosophila counterpart of mammalian pH2AX (Mehrotra and McKim, 2006), to follow the repair of DSBs after IR and found that resolution of these lesions was unaffected in the germaria of p53 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from DNA repair analysis.

claim: The rates at which wild-type and p53−/− GSCs/CBs entered proliferative arrest after IR were indistinguishable.
source: Similarly, in BrdU incorporation studies, the rates at which wild-type and p53−/− GSCs/CBs entered proliferative arrest were also indistinguishable (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is experimental data from BrdU incorporation studies.

claim: In the post-stress period, p53 mutants were significantly delayed for re-entry into the cell cycle.
source: However, in the post-stress period, we did observe that p53 mutants were significantly delayed for re-entry into the cell cycle (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is experimental data from BrdU incorporation studies.

claim: The cell cycle re-entry defect in p53 mutants is reversed in p53 genomic rescue strains.
source: Furthermore, this defect is reversed in p53 genomic rescue strains confirming an assignment of this phenotype to the p53 locus (Figure 4—source data 1B).
evidence: This is experimental validation using genetic rescue.

claim: Wild-type females recovered from infertility within 1 week post-exposure to IR at a dose of 11.5 krad.
source: Figure 4B shows that wild-type females recovered from infertility within 1 week post-exposure to IR at a dose of 11.5 krad.
evidence: This is experimental data from fertility recovery assays.

claim: Females lacking p53 remained permanently infertile even when tracked over 2 weeks after IR at 11.5 krad.
source: In contrast, females lacking p53 remained permanently infertile even when tracked over 2 weeks after IR (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is experimental data from fertility recovery assays.

claim: The sterility defect in p53− females was reversed in p53 genomic rescue strains.
source: We tested two rescue strains and in both cases the sterility defect was reversed (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is experimental validation using genetic rescue.

claim: Neither p53 rescue strain fully restored fertility to wild type levels, possibly reflecting incomplete restoration of wild type regulation in the transgenes.
source: However, neither rescue strain fully restored fertility to wild type levels, possibly reflecting incomplete restoration of wild type regulation in the transgenes.
evidence: This is an observation with speculative interpretation.

claim: After 9 krad IR, p53−/− females exhibit impaired fertility whereas WT flies remained fertile.
source: After this challenge, p53−/− females exhibit impaired fertility, whereas WT flies remained fertile (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is experimental data from fertility assays at intermediate IR dose.

claim: At 9 krad IR, p53−/− stem cells showed persistently reduced proliferative activity even 7 days after IR.
source: Under these conditions, we observed persistently reduced proliferative activity in p53−/− stem cells even 7 days after IR (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C, Figure 4—source data 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data from BrdU incorporation studies.

claim: Fertility defects seen in p53−/− flies are linked to impaired cell cycle kinetics in GSCs.
source: This result is consistent with the possibility that fertility defects seen in p53−/− flies are linked to the impaired cell cycle kinetics found in GSCs.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between cell cycle and fertility defects.

claim: Radiosensitivity associated with the p53−/− genotype applies to germline tissue.
source: Furthermore, the data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A suggest that radiosensitivity associated with the p53−/− genotype, previously been documented for larval stages (Sogame et al., 2003), also applies to germline tissue.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-dependent fertility recovery data, with citation to prior work.

claim: Transient expression of Drosophila RasV12 provoked robust p53 activation mainly in the GSCs and CBs.
source: Transient expression of the Drosophila RasV12 counterpart provoked robust p53 activation mainly in the GSCs and CBs (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from RasV12 overexpression studies.

claim: Cyclin E oncoprotein produced p53 activation similar to RasV12.
source: Figure 5E shows that another oncoprotein, Cyclin E, produced similar results.
evidence: This is experimental data from Cyclin E overexpression studies.

claim: In bam mutants, where a block in differentiation causes extensive hyperplasia, extensive p53 reporter activity was observed.
source: We also examined these biosensors in bam mutants, where a block in differentiation causes extensive hyperplasia (McKearin and Ohlstein, 1995) and in these tumors extensive reporter activity was also seen (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is experimental data from bam mutant analysis with citation to prior work.

claim: Expanded BMP signaling in neighboring somatic cells causes inappropriate growth and robust p53 activity.
source: Likewise, expanded BMP (bone morphogenic protein) signaling (Chen and McKearin, 2003) or reduced Lsd1 (lysine-specific demethylase 1) activity (Eliazer et al., 2011) in neighboring somatic cells can also cause inappropriate growth and robust p53 activity was similarly observed in these germline tumors as well (Figure 5F,G,H).
evidence: This is experimental data from BMP signaling manipulation with citations.

claim: Reduced Lsd1 activity in neighboring somatic cells causes inappropriate growth and robust p53 activity.
source: Likewise, expanded BMP (bone morphogenic protein) signaling (Chen and McKearin, 2003) or reduced Lsd1 (lysine-specific demethylase 1) activity (Eliazer et al., 2011) in neighboring somatic cells can also cause inappropriate growth and robust p53 activity was similarly observed in these germline tumors as well (Figure 5F,G,H).
evidence: This is experimental data from Lsd1 manipulation with citations.

claim: Whether caused by forced oncoprotein expression, failed differentiation programs, or expansion of the stem cell niche, inappropriate growth of Drosophila tissues was consistently accompanied by p53 activity.
source: Therefore, whether caused by forced oncoprotein expression (panels B, E), failed differentiation programs (panels C, D), or expansion of the stem cell niche (panels F–H), inappropriate growth of Drosophila tissues was consistently accompanied by p53 activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from multiple tumor model experiments.

claim: Very few pH2Av foci were observed in bam tumors and these foci did not co-localize with p53 biosensor activity.
source: We observed very few pH2Av foci in bam tumors and, notably, these foci did not co-localize with p53 biosensor activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from pH2Av staining in bam tumors.

claim: p53 activity in bam tumors is not triggered by DSBs but appears to be directly triggered by signals associated with hyperplastic growth.
source: Therefore, p53 activity in these tumors is not triggered by DSBs but instead, appears to be directly triggered by signals associated with hyperplastic growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of pH2Av/p53 colocalization.

claim: Tumor size was not significantly altered in bam−/− ovaries that lacked p53.
source: Tumor size was not significantly altered in the absence of p53, but we did observe dramatically altered cytology in tumors that lacked p53.
evidence: This is experimental observation from bam−/−;p53−/− analysis.

claim: Dramatically altered cytology was observed in bam−/− tumors that lacked p53.
source: Tumor size was not significantly altered in the absence of p53, but we did observe dramatically altered cytology in tumors that lacked p53.
evidence: This is experimental observation from bam−/−;p53−/− analysis.

claim: bam−/− ovarian cysts are typically filled with stem-like cells that exhibit round or dumbbell-shaped fusomes when stained with α-HTS.
source: As seen in Figure 6A, bam−/− ovarian cysts are typically filled with stem-like cells that exhibit round or dumbbell-shaped fusomes when stained with α-HTS (Lin et al., 1994).
evidence: This is experimental observation with citation to the HTS marker.

claim: Defective fusomes were seen in all bam−/−;p53−/− cysts.
source: As documented in Figure 6C, defective fusomes were seen in all bam−/−;p53−/− cysts and, in nearly half of these unusually large nuclei were observed.
evidence: This is quantitative experimental data from bam−/−;p53−/− analysis.

claim: In nearly half of bam−/−;p53−/− cysts, unusually large nuclei were observed.
source: As documented in Figure 6C, defective fusomes were seen in all bam−/−;p53−/− cysts and, in nearly half of these unusually large nuclei were observed.
evidence: This is quantitative experimental data from bam−/−;p53−/− analysis.

claim: Micronuclei were prevalent in bam−/−;p53−/− samples.
source: Though not quantified, micronuclei were also prevalent in these samples.
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from bam−/−;p53−/− analysis.

claim: Defective fusome morphologies and irregular nuclei are consistent with aberrant mitosis.
source: Since defective fusome morphologies and irregular nuclei are consistent with aberrant mitosis, our data suggests a role for p53 in promoting proper cell cycle progression in these stem-like tumors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: p53 has a role in promoting proper cell cycle progression in stem-like tumors.
source: Since defective fusome morphologies and irregular nuclei are consistent with aberrant mitosis, our data suggests a role for p53 in promoting proper cell cycle progression in these stem-like tumors.
evidence: This is inferred from the cytological defects in bam−/−;p53−/− tumors.

claim: 297 gene transcripts were altered by at least twofold or greater in bam−/− ovaries lacking p53.
source: In total, we found that 297 gene transcripts were altered by at least twofold or greater in the absence of p53.
evidence: This is data from microarray analysis.

claim: Among the top 20 genes normally suppressed by p53 in germline tumors, there was a modest enrichment for transcripts absent in either embryonic stages or other somatic tissues.
source: However, among the top 20 genes that are normally suppressed by p53 in these germline tumors, we observed a modest enrichment for transcripts that were absent in either the embryonic stages or other somatic tissues (Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is data from GEXC analysis of microarray results.

claim: p53 exerts functional activities that impact cellular and molecular properties of Drosophila stem cell tumors.
source: These data, together with our histological studies (Figure 6), establish that p53 exerts functional activities that impact cellular and molecular properties of Drosophila stem cell tumors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the combined histological and molecular data.

claim: p53 occupies a central position within conserved stress response networks throughout the animal kingdom.
source: Throughout the animal kingdom, p53 occupies a central position within conserved stress response networks.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: p53 integrates diverse signals associated with DNA damage and uncontrolled proliferation to govern adaptive downstream responses such as increased DNA repair, arrested cell cycle, and apoptosis.
source: The protein integrates diverse signals associated with DNA damage and uncontrolled proliferation to govern adaptive downstream responses such as increased DNA repair, arrested cell cycle, and apoptosis (Vousden and Lane, 2007).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature (Vousden and Lane, 2007).

claim: The genes encoding p53 are not essential for viability.
source: Where examined, the genes encoding p53 are not essential for viability but have been implicated as regulators of aging (Derry et al., 2007; Donehower et al., 1992; Lee et al., 2003; Sogame et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from multiple prior studies.

claim: p53 genes have been implicated as regulators of aging.
source: Where examined, the genes encoding p53 are not essential for viability but have been implicated as regulators of aging (Derry et al., 2007; Donehower et al., 1992; Lee et al., 2003; Sogame et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from multiple prior studies.

claim: Ancestral roles for the p53 gene family must have predated functions in tumor suppression.
source: It is now well appreciated that ancestral roles for this gene family must have predated functions in tumor suppression.
evidence: This is stated as current understanding in the field.

claim: Members of the p53 gene family are present in unicellular protists and short-lived multicellular organisms.
source: In support of this, members of the p53 gene family are present in unicellular protists and short-lived multicellular organisms (Lu et al., 2009; Mendoza et al., 2003; Nordstrom and Abrams, 2000).
evidence: This is cited from multiple prior studies.

claim: Cancer was probably a negligible source of selection pressure during the course of human evolution.
source: Furthermore, cancer was probably a negligible source of selection pressure during the course of human evolution (Aranda-Anzaldo and Dent, 2007) and the combined removal of canonical p53 effectors (p21, Puma, and Noxa) does not account for tumor suppression in mice (Valente et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature.

claim: The combined removal of canonical p53 effectors (p21, Puma, and Noxa) does not account for tumor suppression in mice.
source: Furthermore, cancer was probably a negligible source of selection pressure during the course of human evolution (Aranda-Anzaldo and Dent, 2007) and the combined removal of canonical p53 effectors (p21, Puma, and Noxa) does not account for tumor suppression in mice (Valente et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature (Valente et al., 2013).

claim: Tumor suppressive roles for the p53 family were co-opted from primordial functions, some of which may have been linked to meiotic recombination.
source: These and other observations suggest that tumor suppressive roles for the p53 family were co-opted from primordial functions, some of which may have been linked to meiotic recombination (Lu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation to prior work.

claim: In mammary stem cells p53 promotes asymmetric division and cell polarity, helping to limit the population of stem cells in the mammary gland.
source: For example, in mammary stem cells p53 promotes asymmetric division and cell polarity, thereby helping to limit the population of stem cells in the mammary gland (Cicalese et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature (Cicalese et al., 2009).

claim: Reprogramming of somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) is greatly increased in p53 deficient cells.
source: Furthermore, reprogramming of somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) is greatly increased in p53 deficient cells, suggesting that p53 may act as a 'barrier for induced pluripotency' (Krizhanovsky and Lowe, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature (Krizhanovsky and Lowe, 2009).

claim: p53 may act as a 'barrier for induced pluripotency'.
source: Furthermore, reprogramming of somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) is greatly increased in p53 deficient cells, suggesting that p53 may act as a 'barrier for induced pluripotency' (Krizhanovsky and Lowe, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation cited from prior work.

claim: p53 induces embryonic stem cell differentiation to maintain genomic stability after DNA damage.
source: Consistent with this, several labs have shown that p53 induces embryonic stem cell differentiation to maintain genomic stability after DNA damage (Lin et al., 2005; Neveu et al., 2010; Zhao and Xu, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from multiple prior studies.

claim: An ancestral focus of p53 action could operate in stem cells.
source: Together with recent studies in planaria, these observations indicate that an ancestral focus of p53 action could operate in stem cells (Pearson and Sanchez Alvarado, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from multiple lines of evidence with citation.

claim: When DNA breaks were exogenously imposed or intrinsically engineered, Drosophila p53 (Dp53) was activated selectively in germline stem cells (GSCs) and their immediate daughters.
source: When DNA breaks were exogenously imposed or intrinsically engineered, Drosophila p53 (Dp53) was activated selectively in germline stem cells (GSCs) and their immediate daughters, indicating that these cells are uniquely licensed for p53 action.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study.

claim: GSCs and their immediate daughters are uniquely licensed for p53 action.
source: When DNA breaks were exogenously imposed or intrinsically engineered, Drosophila p53 (Dp53) was activated selectively in germline stem cells (GSCs) and their immediate daughters, indicating that these cells are uniquely licensed for p53 action.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the selective p53 activation pattern.

claim: In various germline tumor models Dp53 was constitutively hyperactivated.
source: Furthermore, in various germline tumor models Dp53 was constitutively hyperactivated, suggesting that ancient links between p53 and inappropriate growth predate canonical effectors that connect these regulatory networks (e.g., ARF and MDM2).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from tumor model experiments.

claim: Ancient links between p53 and inappropriate growth predate canonical effectors that connect these regulatory networks (e.g., ARF and MDM2).
source: Furthermore, in various germline tumor models Dp53 was constitutively hyperactivated, suggesting that ancient links between p53 and inappropriate growth predate canonical effectors that connect these regulatory networks (e.g., ARF and MDM2).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the tumor model findings.

claim: The Drosophila gonad is a classic system for studying the stem cell compartment since stem cells, their immediate daughters, and the surrounding niche are easily identified.
source: The Drosophila gonad is a classic system for studying the stem cell compartment since stem cells, their immediate daughters, and the surrounding niche are easily identified.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Drosophila system.

claim: Stem cell specificity of p53 activation was not an artifact intrinsic to the biosensors.
source: We note that stem cell specificity was not an artifact intrinsic to the biosensors, since independent reporters behaved similarly in both the female and male germline and required the wild-type Dp53 locus in both cases.
evidence: This is stated as validation of the biosensor approach.

claim: Despite being present and activatable throughout the gonad, functional p53 is restricted to stem cells and their immediate progeny by specific genetic determinants.
source: Therefore, despite the fact that it is present and activatable throughout the gonad, functional p53 is restricted to stem cells and their immediate progeny by specific genetic determinants.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the observation that mutants can lose the restriction.

claim: The findings support an intimate and ancient link between p53 and stem cell biology.
source: Collectively, our work supports previous indications that there is an intimate and ancient link between p53 and stem cell biology (Pearson and Sanchez Alvarado, 2009).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion with citation to prior work.

claim: The p53R-GFP biosensor offers opportunities to operationally mark stem cells in the fly germline.
source: Our findings also offer rare and novel opportunities to operationally mark the stem cells in the fly germline, as visualized by p53R-GFP.
evidence: This is stated as an application of the findings.

claim: The p53R-GFP marker is distinct from conventional stem cell labels because it is not constitutively expressed but represents a functional output conditional upon a perturbation.
source: This marker is distinct from conventional stem cell labels (Deng and Lin, 1997) since it is not constitutively expressed but, instead, represents a functional output that is conditional upon a perturbation.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature with citation to conventional markers.

claim: The p53 biosensors may not reflect the full scope of effector output regulated by the p53 network.
source: We further note that like all reporter systems, our p53 biosensors may not reflect the full scope of effector output regulated by this network, and activities visualized here could transmit only subsets of p53-mediated responses.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the biosensor approach.

claim: Stem cells may be acutely sensitive to sources of genomic instability with a higher propensity for engaging adaptive responses relative to other cells.
source: Nevertheless, despite this possible limitation, our results are consistent with suggestions that stem cells may be acutely sensitive to sources of genomic instability with a higher propensity for engaging adaptive responses relative to other cells (Mandal et al., 2011; Sperka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation consistent with prior suggestions, with citations.

claim: In reproductive tissues, the p53 regulatory network is either preferentially licensed in stem cells or selectively blocked outside of this compartment.
source: We propose that in reproductive tissues, the p53 regulatory network is either preferentially licensed in stem cells or selectively blocked outside of this compartment.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: ATR expression was not rate limiting for p53 activation in the germline.
source: Consistent with this idea, ATR expression, was not rate limiting for p53 activation in the germline (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A′, Figure 1—source data 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data from ATR mutant analysis.

claim: p53 induction in GSCs/CBs was independent of the topoisomerase, Spo11.
source: Furthermore, unlike meiotic induction, p53 induction in GSCs/CBs was independent of the topoisomerase, Spo11 (Figure 1—source data 1A; Lu et al, 2010).
evidence: This is experimental data with citation to prior work.

claim: Chk2 is broadly expressed and functionally associated with oocyte development throughout the ovary.
source: Chk2 could contribute to the selective activation in stem cells seen here, but since Chk2 is also broadly expressed and functionally associated with oocyte development throughout the ovary (Abdu et al., 2002; Oishi et al., 1998) any potential role in GSCs must extend beyond a simple presence or absence of this kinase.
evidence: This is cited from prior literature (Abdu et al., 2002; Oishi et al., 1998).

claim: Within detection limits, no obvious connection was observed between p53 status and apoptosis, DNA double-strand break repair, or cell cycle arrest.
